# Optimization and Training Procedures

Also called: Training Strategies for Radiance Fields

## Overview
This family covers the algorithmic procedures, hyperparameter configurations, and optimization loops used to train Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models and their variants. It addresses the problem of converging implicit 3D representations from 2D observations by defining how model parameters are updated, how sampling strategies interact with the optimizer, and how specific architectural modifications (such as last-layer retraining or activation-based skipping) alter the standard training loop. It sets itself apart from [Model Architecture Modifications](11313-model-architecture-modifications.md) by focusing on the *process* of learning (optimization dynamics, learning rates, batch sizes) rather than the *structure* of the network itself, although the two are tightly coupled.

## Shared principles
The core mechanism across all methods in this family is the minimization of a photometric loss, typically Mean Squared Error (MSE), between rendered pixel colors and ground-truth images. The optimization is performed using gradient-based methods, predominantly Adam or AdamW [S1].

Key shared mathematical components include:
1.  **Ray Sampling:** The training loop generates rays from camera poses and samples points along them. The distribution of these samples (uniform, stratified, or importance-sampled) affects the gradient signal.
2.  **Volume Rendering:** The differentiable volume rendering equation is used to compute the predicted color $\hat{C}$ and opacity $\hat{\alpha}$ for each ray, allowing gradients to flow back to the network parameters $\Theta$ [G].
3.  **Loss Function:** The primary loss is:
    $$ L = \sum_{r} \| C_r - \hat{C}_r \|^2 $$
    where $C_r$ is the ground truth color and $\hat{C}_r$ is the rendered color for ray $r$.

## Subtopics

### [Activation-Informed Coarse-to-Fine Rendering](12277-activation-informed-coarse-to-fine-rendering.md)
This method accelerates inference by conditionally skipping the expensive fine-pass evaluation for rays determined to be empty or background. It sets itself apart from standard coarse-to-fine rendering by using intermediate network activation values rather than density thresholds to decide whether to skip the fine pass. It is chosen when inference speed is critical and the scene contains significant background regions, though it may fail on real-world scenes with detailed backgrounds [12277-activation-informed-coarse-to-fine-rendering.md].

### [Last Layer Re-training](13532-last-layer-re-training.md)
This technique propagates color edits from a single view to an entire pre-trained NeRF by retraining only the last layer of the color MLP. It sets itself apart from full retraining (which is expensive and risks destroying view-dependent effects) and methods like ICE-NeRF (which suffer from color bleeding) by freezing the geometric and view-dependent structure in earlier layers. It is chosen for rapid, localized color editing [13532-last-layer-re-training.md].

### Rip-NeRF Optimization
Rip-NeRF optimization involves training tiny MLP weights and ripmaps $R$. Model weights are initialized using Glorot and Bengio (2010) initialization, while ripmaps $R$ are initialized from a uniform distribution over $[-0.01, 0.01]$. The optimizer used is AdamW. The base learning rate is $2 \times 10^{-3}$, scaled by 10x for the ripmaps $R$ due to their direct scene representation role. The learning rate schedule reduces the rate by 0.6x at steps 60K, 90K, 100K, and 108K, over a total of 120K iterations. The batch size is dynamically adjusted to maintain approximately 256K spheres per batch [S1].

## Background
The standard NeRF training loop was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020 [G]. Subsequent works have modified these procedures to address specific challenges: inference speed (Activation-Informed Coarse-to-Fine), editing capabilities (Last Layer Re-training), and anti-aliasing/efficiency (Rip-NeRF). The use of AdamW and specific learning rate schedules has become standard in modern radiance field optimization [S1].
